newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Rally in world coffee at new highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rally in world coffee at new highs.

text.p: Coffee futures defied analysts' expectations that they might take a respite from their blistering rally on Thursday and set to carving fresh highs again.
Elsewhere on world commodity markets copper rose in value on the London Metal Exchange but gold suffered from reports of a likely revaluation of German bullion reserves.

After a quiet morning's trading in London, with analysts expecting coffee futures to settle, new gains in New York's early session prompted a return to the longest unbroken rally the commodity has seen in two decades.
Coffee futures again made highs not seen since frost last hit Brazil, back in 1994, even though this year's season for frost scares has yet to begin.
The May contract for the high quality arabica bean traded in New York rose to a life-of-contract high at $2.79 per pound. Arabica futures prices have doubled in 1997.
The news that Latin American supply is tight and American stocks of the higher quality arabica coffee beans are at 20-year lows has sent speculators on a buying spree.

The latest supply concerns were an announcement of a production deficit by top producer Brazil and word that number two producer Columbia had effectively tossed its official, regulated price out of the window.

Brazil's Coffee Exporters' Association (Abecafe) said it expected to see a production deficit that it will have to meet from stocks of around four million 60-kg bags in 1997/98 despite a higher second crop estimate of 24 million 60-kg bags.
"A crop of around 24 million bags compares with a demand, between exports and internal demand, of 28 million bags a year," Abecafe said in a statement.

Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the National Coffee Growers' Federation had been authorised to pay any price necessary to supply itself with fresh coffee to meet its export commitments.
On Monday, the federation's general manager, Jorge Cardenas said it was having "enormous difficulties" meeting export commitments due to unusually low supply.
"The federation has been left without fresh coffee," Ocampo said. "They have coffee in stocks but part of the commitments, the majority, have to be fulfilled with fresh coffee."
The London traded futures for robusta bean types, used mainly in soluble or instant blends, have also hit contract highs as funds made the most of the supply fears.

The benchmark July robusta contract jumped $70 to $1,940 a tonne in afternoon trading to notch up the third year-high in as many days. Robustas have already risen by more than 50 percent since the start of the year.
Western firms that have already had to lift retail prices because of the world rally include Folgers in the United States and Douwe Egberts, owned by U.S. giant Sara Lee Corp, in Europe.
On the London Metal Exchange copper stole the day.

A pre-market rally attributed variously to a 3,225-tonne drop in LME stocks, potential labour problems in Chile and fund interest helped push the metal above $2,440 a tonne - the highest the market has been since early June 1996.
Three months was at $2,447/50 a tonne, well above the $2,414 Wednesday official close, spurred higher by speculative investment fund buying overnight, traders said.
This trend was likely to continue, as nearby copper supplies are thin and demand is brisk.
"Copper looks very good right now, because that $2,440 level was very important. If it can stay above here it has much farther to go," a trader said.
The market was keeping an eye on developments at Chile's big Chuquicamata copper mines, where unions representing supervisors were in talks to renew a pay deal which expires at the end of the month.
Gold eased as the market reacted to reports that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel would be discussing a proposal to revalue the country's gold reserves.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were up a couple of cents a bushel on a U.S. Department of Agriculture weekly export sales report which detailed a larger-than-expected rise in crop sales.
